summary: Updates the specification of CUBIC, a TCP congestion control algorithm that grows the window with a cubic function, to include improvements from implementations and academic work. It is the default in Linux, Windows, and Apple stacks.

eli5.summary: A way for computers to speed up sending data carefully, going fast when safe and slowing near the point where trouble starts.

subtitle: The TCP congestion control algorithm that grows its sending window along a cubic curve, built for fast, long-distance networks.

tldr.problem: Classic Reno congestion control grows its congestion window by a fixed step each round trip, so after a loss it recovers very slowly on networks with a large bandwidth-delay product.
tldr.mechanism: CUBIC grows the window as a cubic function of the time since the last congestion event. It climbs fast, flattens near the old maximum, then probes gently beyond it, and it falls back to Reno-like growth where Reno would do better.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9438 moves CUBIC to the Standards Track, obsoletes RFC 8312 and updates RFC 5681. The text says CUBIC is the default TCP congestion control in the Linux, Windows and Apple stacks.

today: RFC 9438 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023 that obsoletes RFC 8312 and updates RFC 5681. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it. The text says CUBIC is the default TCP congestion control in the Linux, Windows and Apple stacks.

sections.title: Why CUBIC Exists
sections.content:
RFC 9438 specifies CUBIC, a TCP congestion control algorithm. It was designed because classical Reno (RFC 5681) uses very little of a fast, long-distance path. Reno raises its congestion window (cwnd) linearly after a congestion event, which is slow when the bandwidth-delay product (BDP) is large. The RFC notes that this shows up even at window sizes of several hundred packets.

CUBIC replaces the linear increase with a cubic function to improve scalability and stability. The RFC says it can also serve as the default congestion controller for other transports such as QUIC (RFC 9000) and SCTP (RFC 9260).

This document updates the earlier specification, RFC 8312, with improvements from the Linux, Windows and Apple implementations and from academic work. Because CUBIC can be more aggressive than RFC 5681 allows, the RFC also replaces the first paragraph of Section 3 of that document with a normative reference to guideline (1) in Section 3 of RFC 5033.

The RFC states that CUBIC was widely deployed before it followed the process in RFC 5033. The IETF decided to publish it on the Standards Track because of its long Internet-scale deployment experience.
sections.eli5: Old-style sending speeds up one tiny step at a time, like filling a swimming pool with a teaspoon. CUBIC takes bigger scoops when it is safe.

sections.title: The Four Design Principles
sections.content:
The RFC lists four principles behind CUBIC.

  • Concave then convex growth. CUBIC remembers the window size at the last congestion event and grows toward it along the concave part of a cubic curve. It plateaus there, then switches to the convex part. Most samples sit close to the remembered size, which the RFC ties to high utilization and stability.
  • Reno-friendliness. In networks with short RTTs and small bandwidth, where Reno works well, CUBIC behaves like Reno. The RFC calls this the Reno-friendly region.
  • RTT-fairness. Two CUBIC flows with different RTTs get a throughput ratio that is linearly proportional to the inverse of their RTT ratio.
  • A balanced decrease factor. CUBIC sets its multiplicative decrease factor to 0.7, where Reno uses 0.5. The RFC admits a side effect: slower convergence, especially under low statistical multiplexing.
sections.eli5: CUBIC wants to be fast on big, long roads, polite to older drivers who share the road, and fair to cars coming from near and far. It backs off only a little after a bump.

sections.title: The Window Increase Function
sections.content:
During congestion avoidance CUBIC uses W_cubic(t) = C * (t - K)^3 + W_max. Here t is the time in seconds since the current congestion avoidance stage began, W_max is the window size just before the last reduction, and K is the time the function takes to climb back to W_max if there is no further congestion event. The constant C sets how aggressive CUBIC is against other algorithms in high-BDP networks. Window sizes are counted in segments of the sender maximum segment size (SMSS).

On each new ACK CUBIC computes a target window for one smoothed RTT in the future, from W_cubic(t + RTT). The target is clamped: it is never below cwnd and never above 1.5 * cwnd. The time t MUST NOT include periods when cwnd was not updated because the flow was application-limited.

CUBIC then works in one of three regions and takes the larger of W_cubic(t) and the Reno estimate W_est:

  • Reno-friendly region: when W_cubic(t) is below W_est, cwnd SHOULD be set to W_est. The RFC derives the additive factor from the average window of an AIMD algorithm so that CUBIC matches Reno's average window.
  • Concave region: cwnd is below W_max. On each new ACK, cwnd MUST grow by (target - cwnd) / cwnd.
  • Convex region: cwnd is at or above W_max. The same increment applies, but growth starts very slowly and gradually speeds up, in what the RFC calls the maximum probing phase.
sections.eli5: After a bump, CUBIC speeds up fast, eases off as it nears the old trouble spot, then slowly creeps past it to check whether the road got wider.

sections.title: Reacting to Congestion Events
sections.content:
Multiplicative decrease. When a congestion event is detected (duplicate ACKs, ECN-Echo ACKs, RACK-TLP or QUIC loss detection), CUBIC updates W_max and cuts cwnd and ssthresh at once. The factor beta_cubic SHOULD be 0.7. The new ssthresh is based on the amount of data in flight, and it has a floor of 2 SMSS. For ECN-Echo signals, CUBIC MUST keep reducing cwnd down to 1 SMSS, and if signals persist it MUST slow further, for example with a retransmission timer that backs off exponentially.

Fast convergence. When a flow's cwnd is below its previous W_max, fast convergence SHOULD be implemented: W_max is reduced further so the flow plateaus earlier and leaves room for a new flow. With only one CUBIC flow and no other traffic it SHOULD be disabled.

Timeout. CUBIC reduces cwnd as Reno does, but sets ssthresh using beta_cubic. The next congestion avoidance stage starts with K set to 0.

Spurious events. Reordering can trick a sender into treating a late ACK as loss. An implementation MAY detect spurious timeouts (for example with F-RTO, RFC 5682) and spurious fast retransmits (with TCP Timestamps or D-SACK). It MAY save its state before a reduction and restore it if the loss proves spurious.

Slow start. While cwnd is no more than ssthresh, CUBIC MUST use slow start. It SHOULD use HyStart++ (RFC 9406) and MAY use Reno slow start where HyStart++ is not suitable.
sections.eli5: When CUBIC hits trouble, it slows down to 70 percent of its speed instead of half. If it is going slower than before, it gives a little extra room to newcomers.

sections.title: Fairness and Performance
sections.content:
Section 5 checks CUBIC against the safety guidelines of RFC 5033. Comparison tables in the RFC show that, with a short RTT, CUBIC with a low C matches Reno where Reno already performs well. The RFC says C SHOULD be 0.4, and that a very low value like 0.04 is NOT RECOMMENDED because it cannot use fast, long-distance networks efficiently.

For spare capacity, the RFC's table says that to sustain 10 Gbps with 1500-byte packets and an RTT of 0.1 seconds, Reno needs a loss rate of 2.0e-10, while CUBIC needs 2.9e-8. In other words, CUBIC tolerates far more loss at high rates.

Limits are stated too. CUBIC is loss-based, so it can fill large drop-tail buffers faster than Reno and raise the risk of a standing queue. Like Reno, it suffers where packet loss is a poor sign of bandwidth use, such as wireless or mobile networks. It does not grow cwnd for application-limited flows, and it modifies only window adjustment, so congestion collapse protection is the same as Reno's.

CUBIC needs changes only at the sender. A CUBIC sender works with Reno receivers, and no router changes or help are required.
sections.eli5: CUBIC shares the road fairly with older drivers on short trips, but on a long, empty highway it gets up to speed much sooner. It only needs the driver to change, not the road.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
CUBIC makes no changes to the underlying security of a transport protocol and inherits the concerns in RFC 5681. An attacker who drops or injects ACKs could force a CUBIC sender to cut its bandwidth, or convince it there is no congestion when there is, and so use it as an attack vector against other hosts. The RFC says these attacks are not new to CUBIC and apply to any transport protocol like TCP.

CUBIC introduces no new entities or signals, so its exposure to misbehaving nodes and outside attackers is unchanged from Reno. The document asks IANA to do nothing.
sections.eli5: A trickster who fiddles with the delivery receipts could make CUBIC slow down or go too fast. That trick works on the old way of sending too, so CUBIC is no easier to fool.

items.title: Reno-friendly
items.text: W_cubic(t) is below W_est, so cwnd follows the Reno estimate.

items.title: Concave
items.text: cwnd is below W_max and climbs toward the plateau.

items.title: Convex
items.text: cwnd is at or above W_max and probes slowly for more capacity.
